metadata.title: Reading fiction and theory of mind in early adolescence: concurrent and longitudinal relations

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study uses a longitudinal cohort of children in Birmingham, UK, drawing reading habits and motivation from the PIRLS student questionnaire administered at multiple time points (Time 1–Time 4). The analysis is based on path analysis in Mplus with a maximum likelihood estimator with robust standard errors (MLR) and uses all available data under a missing-at-random assumption, rather than applying ILSA-style complex survey weights. The manuscript does not report any use of PIRLS sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the design is not an international representative sample in the way PIRLS microdata are typically analyzed. Therefore, results should be interpreted as associations within this local cohort, not as population-representative estimates for the UK or for PIRLS participating countries.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a theory-of-mind score derived from the Silent Films task (0–12), and the reading measures come from PIRLS questionnaires and other standardized tests (e.g., YARC, BPVS-3), not from PIRLS achievement scales that would use PV-based scoring. Missing data handling is described as using all available data under a missing-at-random assumption in Mplus (MLR), which corresponds to model-based handling rather than explicit PV combining or a documented imputation method; the paper does not provide a full imputation protocol. Given this, the missing-data strategy is treated as not fully reportable at the level of a specific imputation algorithm, but the analysis clearly does not use listwise deletion.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were selected from an ongoing longitudinal literacy and vocabulary study based in Birmingham, UK. Children with written consent from parents/carers were eligible. Data were collected at four time points spanning the end of primary school and start of secondary school: Time 1 (age 11; n=299), Time 2 (n=266), Time 3 (n=236; main analytic sample), and a smaller Time 4 subsample (n=96) used only for robustness checks. Due to COVID-19 school closures, the full cohort could not be tested at Time 4; Time 4 was excluded from main analyses. For the main models, the authors estimated parameters using all available data for children who participated at Time 3 and at least one previous wave (n=236), assuming data were missing at random.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS the study leveraged Reading motivation, Receptive vocabulary (BPVS-3), Reading comprehension (YARC) to predict predict ToM at Time 3, finding that This paper is not an ML predictive modeling study; it examines concurrent and longitudinal associations between reading fiction and theory of mind (ToM) in a local longitudinal cohort of 236 children in Birmingham, UK (ages 11–13). Reading fiction and non-fiction time were measured using the PIRLS student questionnaire at Time 1 and Time 3, while ToM was measured at Time 3 (and Time 4 for robustness) using the Silent Films task scored 0–12. The authors used path analysis in Mplus with robust standard errors (MLR) and estimated models using all available data under a missing-at-random assumption. In the concurrent model, ToM at Time 3 was uniquely associated with fiction reading (b=0.26, SE=0.09, 95% CI [0.11, 0.40]) after controlling for verbal ability, reading motivation, age, gender, and parental education; non-fiction reading was not uniquely associated (b=-0.01, SE=0.07). In the longitudinal model, Time 1 fiction and non-fiction reading did not uniquely predict ToM at Time 3; instead, ToM was uniquely associated with receptive vocabulary, parental education, and gender. Limitations include the absence of prior ToM measurement and the use of a single ToM task, so causal direction cannot be inferred. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The study is an empirical developmental psychology paper using path analysis rather than machine learning for prediction/classification, so no ML algorithms, PV handling, or ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are applicable. Consequently, main_findings is left empty because the schema requires StructuredFinding rows for distinct ML target variables, which are not present in this paper’s analytical approach.
